description: TwinTerra uses real NASA data to find new places on Earth that best match the Moon and Mars. Led by a heat transfer researcher, we compare thermal fingerprints, terrain, and ice, not just looks, and will build an interactive analog map. Join us to learn planetary physics with real data!
summary: Team TwinTerra (consisting of one Engineering Professor who is also a NASA Faculty Fellow, and one PhD student in Mechanical Engineering at Northeastern University) is developing an interactive tool that searches the globe for new places on Earth that resemble candidate Moon base and Mars landing sites. Instead of relying on how a place looks, TwinTerra compares the physics. It matches thermal fingerprints, such as thermal inertia, day and night temperature swings, and illumination, along with terrain, surface composition, and ice. Thermal inertia from NASA MODIS data on Earth is compared directly with THEMIS data on Mars and Diviner data on the Moon. Each site gets an analog fingerprint that shows where it matches the Moon or Mars and where the match breaks down, including conditions Earth cannot reproduce, such as low gravity and the radiation environment. We check the method against known analogs like Haughton Crater and Death Valley, then identify less-studied sites on Earth. Good analog sites let engineers test landers, rovers, and construction methods on Earth before missions fly, which lowers cost and risk for future exploration of the Moon and Mars.
details:
What it does and how it works
TwinTerra is an interactive web tool that searches Earth for places that physically resemble candidate Moon base and Mars landing sites. For each target, such as Artemis south pole regions, Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Arcadia Planitia, we build a feature vector across six dimensions: thermal inertia and temperature range, terrain (elevation, slope, roughness), surface composition and emissivity, aridity, ice and water, and dust and wind. We compute the same features on a global grid over Earth and score similarity one dimension at a time. Users choose a purpose (landing tests, rover tests, ice prospecting, or habitability), which changes the weights. Clicking any location shows its analog fingerprint, a radar chart of where it matches and where it does not.

Benefits and intended impact
Engineers need Earth sites to test landers, rovers, construction methods, and resource prospecting before flight. TwinTerra makes finding these sites systematic and explainable, and it points to promising places that have received little attention. Because every score is broken out by dimension, scientists can choose sites for a specific test instead of relying on general resemblance. The tool is open, so students and the public can explore it too.

How it is creative
Most analog searches compare how places look. We compare how they behave. Our team lead is a heat transfer researcher, so we built the method around thermal inertia, a physical property that reflects grain size, rock abundance, and compaction. It can be measured on all three worlds: estimated from MODIS day and night temperatures and albedo on Earth, mapped by THEMIS on Mars, and derived from Diviner temperatures on the Moon. This links the three bodies with physics rather than pictures.

Factors we considered
We validate the method by checking that known analogs, Haughton Crater and Death Valley. We treat scale carefully, scoring specific craters, valleys, and basins rather than whole deserts. Every site lists where the analogy breaks down, including what Earth cannot reproduce: low gravity (0.17 g on the Moon, 0.38 g on Mars), vacuum or a very thin atmosphere, and surface radiation without magnetic shielding. We also note differences in data resolution between Earth and planetary datasets.

Tools and software
Python (NumPy, pandas, xarray, rasterio, scikit-learn), Google Earth Engine, NASA Earthdata and AppEEARS, the Planetary Data System and USGS Astrogeology for Moon and Mars data, QGIS, and GitHub for code and hosting. No special hardware was used.
